newsitem.title: CANADA: Forex traders see no change to EMU start date - poll.
newsitem.headline: Forex traders see no change to EMU start date - poll.

text.p: Traders at this year's ACI foreign exchange congress reckoned Germany's controversial gold reserve revaluation plan will have no material impact on the start date for European monetary union (EMU).

In a poll of 15 traders conducted by Reuters, 13 said the plan is either neutral in terms of the January 1, 1999 start date or could in fact ease the path of monetary union. Only two thought the Bundesbank's strident opposition to Bonn's plans would lead to a delay.
"I know Germany has been taking a hard line but people can't be surprised at this after what Italy and France have done to meet the (Maastricht) criteria."

Traders reckoned Germany's gold plan made a broad based EMU much more likely as it give the green light to other countries to take a more flexible approach with creative accounting in order to qualify for EMU.
"If Germany goes ahead with the revaluation it can hardly turn round to others and tell them they can't do similar things," said a U.S. bank trader.
The traders were attending the 39th International Congress of the Association Cambistie Internationale (ACI) - The Financial Markets Association in Toronto.

Traders were clearly backing the politicians over the central banks and their reaction was at odds with many newspapers and pundits who are now openly talking about a delay, given the dramatic row that has broken out between the Bundesbank and Bonn.
"To be honest it was pretty obvious that either books started to be cooked or goalposts started to be moved," said one senior trader at a leading Spanish bank.

Even Bundesbank board member Wendelin Hartmann, who was speaking at the conference, said while "creative accounting should not be rewarded" he "...personally believed that (EMU) postponment was not a good idea."
The poll also showed that traders are relaxed about the situation in France, where the poor showing in the first round of elections led the unpopular Alain Juppe to resign as Prime Minister.
Traders said even if Lionel Jospin's socialists win in Sunday's second round of elections, the timetable for EMU will remain in place.
Jospin supports a single currency but wants no more fiscal tightening in order to meet the critera, plus initial entry for Italy and Spain.

"If you accept that what Germany is doing opens the door to others to be less austere on the fiscal front you must believe that EMU will go ahead on time and be broadly based," said one U.K. bank trader.
"So long as Bonn holds out and overrules the Bundesbank on the gold thing, they will have to accept a less hard-line approach to others like France and Italy," he added.
He noted that the German government had overruled the Bundesbank on the rate of exchange between Ostmarks and Deutschemarks during German unification.
"They have overruled them once and (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl's big project is monetary union. They will surely overrule them again," the trader added.
